concept.name: TED spread
concept.definition: The spread between the 3-month LIBOR based on US dollars and the 3-month US Treasury bill yield, historically used as a gauge of perceived credit risk in the interbank market versus risk-free government debt. The FRED series (TEDRATE) was discontinued in January 2022 when 3-month USD LIBOR ceased publication; SOFR-based spreads are the suggested modern analogue.
concept.intuition: It measures how much extra interest banks demand to lend to each other compared with what the US government pays — a fear gauge for bank credit risk.
concept.mechanics: Computed daily as TED = 3-month USD LIBOR minus 3-month T-bill rate. Widening signals rising interbank credit/liquidity stress (as in 2008, when it spiked from tens of basis points to over 450); narrowing signals normalizing bank credit conditions. Eurodollar futures on LIBOR were the futures-market leg of the original trade.
concept.formula: TED spread = r_3M_LIBOR - r_3M_Tbill, in percentage points (FRED series TEDRATE, daily, percent).
concept.failure_modes: The measure died with its input: USD LIBOR was removed from FRED on January 31, 2022, so the classic TED spread no longer updates and historical comparisons must be spliced with SOFR-based spreads. Even historically, LIBOR was a survey-based rate subject to manipulation and thinning interbank volumes, distorting the signal.
concept.misconceptions: The TED spread was never a measure of stock-market or inflation risk — it specifically priced interbank unsecured credit versus sovereign risk. A low TED spread did not prove banks were healthy, only that measured LIBOR-Treasury differentials were narrow.
concept.example: In October 2008 the TED spread widened above 4.5 percentage points as LIBOR spiked on counterparty fear while T-bill yields collapsed on safe-haven demand — an extreme reading of interbank stress.
